title: First impressions
goals: Tell anecdotes accurately by combining past simple, past continuous, past perfect and past perfect continuous.
Talk about past habits and situations with used to and would, and tell when each one is possible.
Distinguish be used to (to be accustomed to) from get used to (to become accustomed to) and from used to + infinitive.
Describe people with nuance, using compound personality adjectives and modifiers (rather, a touch, not exactly).
Use collocations with impression (make, leave, create, give, be under the impression) and verbs such as strike and come across as.
Write and tell anecdotes and descriptions of people of 250 to 350 words, well structured and with narrative rhythm.

learn.title: Narrative tenses and past perfect continuous
learn.html:
A good anecdote in English combines four tenses, each with a different role. The past simple moves the story forward (I opened the door); the past continuous paints the background or an action in progress (it was raining); the past perfect steps back to something already finished earlier (she had left); and the past perfect continuous steps back to an activity that had been going on up to that point (she had been waiting).

Form: had been + verb-ing, the same for all persons. Negative: hadn't been. Question: Had she been waiting?

UseExampleNuance
Duration up to a point in the pastI had been waiting for an hour when she showed up.Equivalent to “I had been waiting for an hour”.
Cause of a visible past situationHer hands were covered in flour; she had been baking.It explains what can be seen or felt.
Activity (process) vs. resultShe had been painting the hall (was she still halfway through?) / She had painted the hall (finished).The continuous focuses on the process; the simple focuses on the result or the quantity.

Depth and register. With how long, for and since, the continuous is preferred; with quantities (three emails) or results, the simple: She had written three reports. Stative verbs (know, be, belong, understand) do not usually take the continuous: I had known him for years, not had been knowing. Had been wanting / meaning / hoping to is also acceptable to stress the waiting. In Spanish we use the imperfect tense (“I had been waiting”, “I had been waiting for a while”), which is why Spanish speakers tend to say was waiting for two hours, which in English does not convey that the waiting had started earlier.

In elegant narrative, avoid overusing the past perfect: using it once is enough to fix the “earlier time”, and afterwards you can keep to the past simple if the order is already clear.

watch.wrong: I was waiting for two hours when she finally arrived.
watch.right: I had been waiting for two hours when she finally arrived.
watch.why: The waiting started before the moment you mark: you need had been + -ing.

watch.wrong: By then, she had been knowing the city for years.
watch.right: By then, she had known the city for years.
watch.why: Know is a stative verb: it is not used in the continuous.

watch.wrong: When we got there, the guests already left.
watch.right: When we got there, the guests had already left.
watch.why: An action that happened before another action in the past requires the past perfect.

watch.wrong: He had been writing three emails when I called.
watch.right: He had written three emails when I called.
watch.why: With a specific number or result, use the simple, not the continuous.

learn.title: Past habits: used to and would
learn.html:
Both refer to what was habitual in the past and no longer is, but they are not interchangeable.

used to + basewould + base
Repeated habitsWe used to swim every morning.We would swim every morning.
States (be, have, like, live, know…)I used to be shy. / She used to have long hair.Not possible with stative verbs: I would be shy is incorrect.
Time frameIt does not need one.It needs the past to be already established: When I was a boy, we would…
Negative / questionI didn't use to like it. Did you use to…?Unnatural in the negative; rare in questions.

Nuances. Would is more narrative and nostalgic: it creates scenes (On Sundays my grandfather would put on his hat and walk us to the square). Used to is neutral and works to contrast with the present (He used to smoke; now he doesn't). When would is stressed in speech, it also criticises an annoying habit: He would leave his dirty cups everywhere.

Limits. Used to describes what was repeated or permanent, not a closed period with an exact duration: we do not say I used to live there for five years, but I lived there for five years. It is not used for single actions either. In the past tense, use use to (without -d) after did / didn't.

Contrast with Spanish: the imperfect (“I lived”, “I used to go”) covers all these cases. English has no single equivalent of the imperfect; its meaning is shared between the past simple, used to, would and the past continuous.

watch.wrong: When I was little I would have a bike with training wheels.
watch.right: When I was little I used to have a bike with training wheels.
watch.why: Have in the sense of possession is a state: it only accepts used to.

watch.wrong: She didn't used to like coffee.
watch.right: She didn't use to like coffee.
watch.why: After did/didn't the verb goes in the base form: use to, without -d.

watch.wrong: I used to live in Puebla for five years.
watch.right: I lived in Puebla for five years.
watch.why: A closed period with an exact duration requires the past simple.

watch.wrong: In my twenties I would be very insecure.
watch.right: In my twenties I used to be very insecure.
watch.why: Be is a stative verb: would is not possible.

learn.title: be used to, get used to and used to
learn.html:
Three structures that are almost identical in form and completely different in meaning.

StructureMeaningExample
used to + infinitivePast habit or state that no longer existsI used to get up at five.
be used to + -ing / nounTo be accustomed to (current or past state)I'm used to getting up at five.
get used to + -ing / nounTo become accustomed to (process)It took me weeks to get used to getting up at five.

Grammatical key: in be/get used to, the word to is a preposition, so what follows is a noun or a verb in -ing. In used to + base, by contrast, to is part of the infinitive. A useful test: if you can replace it with a noun (I'm used to the noise), it is the prepositional structure.

Flexibility. Be used to and get used to can be conjugated in any tense: I'll never get used to the noise; she has got (gotten) used to the cold; he wasn't used to being interrupted. They can be intensified: I'm very / quite / not at all used to…; I'm getting used to… expresses a process in progress.

Register. In formal contexts you will see be accustomed to / become accustomed to with the same meaning: The staff are accustomed to working under pressure.

watch.wrong: I'm not used to wake up so early.
watch.right: I'm not used to waking up so early.
watch.why: In be used to, to is a preposition: it is followed by -ing.

watch.wrong: When I was a child, I was used to play in the street.
watch.right: When I was a child, I used to play in the street.
watch.why: For a finished past habit, use used to + base.

watch.wrong: I'm getting used to drive on the left.
watch.right: I'm getting used to driving on the left.
watch.why: Get used to + -ing, just like be used to.

watch.wrong: He isn't use to spicy food.
watch.right: He isn't used to spicy food.
watch.why: Be used to takes the participle used (with -d); it is not use to.

learn.title: Describing people with nuance
learn.html:
At C1 level it is not enough to say He is nice / She is difficult: you are expected to grade, soften and qualify your descriptions, especially when criticising someone or talking about someone you have only just met.

ResourceExamplesEffect
Softeners: rather, fairly, somewhat, a touch, slightly, a bitHe's rather reserved. She's a touch too blunt.They soften the statement; rather and somewhat are more formal than a bit.
Understatement: not exactly, not the most + adjectiveHe's not exactly punctual. She's not the most tactful person.They criticise with irony and politeness.
Impression: seem, come across as, strike me as, give the impression ofShe comes across as confident. He struck me as a little aloof.They separate appearance from reality.
Tendency: tend to, the sort of person whoHe tends to talk over people. She's the sort of person who remembers every birthday.They generalise without being categorical.

Gradable and extreme adjectives. Gradable adjectives (tired, good, interesting) accept very, rather, a bit. Extreme or absolute adjectives (exhausted, brilliant, fascinating, terrified) already contain the intensity and are reinforced with absolutely, utterly, completely, totally, not with very: absolutely exhausted, but very tired.

Syntax. After come across as and strike me as comes an adjective or a noun phrase, never an adverb. After seem comes an adjective or to be, never being. In Spanish one verb covers all of this; in English, look refers to appearance, while seem / come across refer to the overall impression.

watch.wrong: He's very exhausted after the flight.
watch.right: He's absolutely exhausted after the flight.
watch.why: Exhausted is an extreme adjective: it is reinforced with absolutely/utterly, not with very.
Come across as takes an adjective, not an adverb.

watch.wrong: He seemed being a little nervous.
watch.right: He seemed (to be) a little nervous.
watch.why: Seem + adjective or seem + to be; never seem being.

watch.wrong: She made me an impression of being very honest.
watch.right: She gave me the impression of being very honest.
watch.why: The collocation is give someone the impression of / make an impression on someone.

learn.title: Functions: telling anecdotes and describing with caution
learn.html:
• Setting the scene: It was a stifling afternoon in July, and I had been queuing for an hour…
  • Moving the story on: Out of the blue… / Just then… / Before I knew it… / The next thing I knew…
  • Adding a twist: As it turned out… / To my surprise… / Little did I realise… (this last one is studied with inversion in unit 10).
  • Showing your reaction: I was taken aback. / It dawned on me that… / I couldn't help laughing.
  • Hedging an opinion of a person: He struck me as rather… / If I'm honest, she comes across as a touch… / I may be wrong, but…
  • Correcting a first impression: I couldn't have been more wrong. / I soon warmed to her. / Appearances can be deceptive.
  • Wrapping up: To cut a long story short… / The upshot was that… / Looking back, …

write.prompt: Describe a person who made a strong first impression on you and whose true character turned out to be different (or exactly as you expected). Write 250-350 words. Explain what you noticed at first, how you judged them, what changed your mind, and what you think now. Use at least four compound adjectives of personality and several hedging devices (rather, a touch, not exactly, tend to).
targets: come across as / strike me as / give the impression
checklist: 250-350 words in 3-4 well-connected paragraphs
At least one correct use of had been + -ing
At least one past habit with used to or would (no would with stative verbs)
Four compound personality adjectives used well
Two or more softeners (rather, a touch, not exactly, tend to)
One collocation with impression and come across as / strike me as + adjective
A narrative connector (as it turned out, to my surprise) and a closing reflection
write.model:
When I first met Elena, my university tutor, she struck me as rather cold and a touch intimidating. She had been working in the department for almost twenty years, and she carried herself with the kind of composure that tends to keep students at a distance. Her office was spotless, her emails were curt, and she made a point of never smiling during lectures. My first impression, I am embarrassed to say, was that she was a narrow-minded, hard-nosed academic with little patience for a nervous newcomer.

I kept that opinion for the best part of a term. Whenever I handed in an essay, she would return it covered in red ink, and I used to dread the moment she called my name. In class she came across as sharp and not exactly approachable, and I assumed her comments were designed to expose our weaknesses rather than to help us.

As it turned out, I could hardly have been more mistaken. One evening I stayed late in the library, panicking over a deadline, and Elena, who had been marking papers in the next room for hours, came in and sat down beside me. She spent nearly an hour talking me through my argument and, to my surprise, she was warm, quick-witted and genuinely funny. I later learned that she had been quietly paying for a struggling student's textbooks for two years. Far from being cold, she was big-hearted and strong-willed, and her severity was simply her way of expecting the best from us.

Looking back, the episode taught me to distrust the impression people give in the first five minutes. Reserve is often mistaken for hostility, and I now tend to withhold judgement until I have seen someone under pressure. Elena remains one of the most formative people I have ever met, and I am rather ashamed that it took me a whole term to realise it.

write.prompt: Tell the story of a time you moved to a new place, started a new job or joined a new group of people. Write 250-350 words. Describe what life was like before (used to / would), how long you had been preparing or waiting, how strange it felt at first, and how you gradually got used to it. Include at least one moment that caught you off guard.
checklist: 250-350 words with a beginning, middle and end
Past perfect (continuous) for what happened before the start of the story
Be used to / get used to + -ing or noun, at least twice
Used to / would to contrast with the earlier life
Four expressions from the Telling an anecdote block (out of the blue, taken aback, to make matters worse...)
Avoid overusing the past perfect: return to the past simple when the order is already clear
A closing reflection (Looking back, ...)
write.model:
Two years ago I moved from a small town in the north to Madrid to take up a position at an engineering firm. For months I had been preparing for the change: I had been saving money, studying the neighbourhoods and, if I am honest, convincing myself that nothing would really be different. Back home I used to walk to work in ten minutes, and on Sundays we would all gather at my grandmother's house for lunch. I was used to knowing everyone in the bakery by name.

The first few weeks were disorienting. I was not used to commuting for an hour on a crowded metro, and the noise kept me awake at night. Out of the blue, on my second Monday, my manager asked me to present our project to the entire board. I was completely taken aback; nobody had mentioned it, and I had barely finished unpacking my boxes. To make matters worse, my laptop crashed ten minutes before the meeting. As luck would have it, a colleague lent me hers, and, to my relief, the presentation went better than I had expected.

Little by little, things fell into place. I found a café where the owner began to greet me by name, I joined a climbing group, and I stopped counting the days until my next trip home. By the spring I had got used to living among strangers, and I even began to enjoy the anonymity. I no longer noticed the noise, and I had learned to treat the metro as thinking time.

Looking back, what surprised me most was not how hard the beginning was, but how quickly the unfamiliar became ordinary. I still miss those Sunday lunches, but I have come to see that being a newcomer taught me to be more adaptable, and more patient with myself.

reading.title: The Fifteen-Second Verdict
reading.intro: Read the opinion article and answer the questions.
paragraphs: I have always prided myself on being a good judge of character. Walk me into a room, introduce me to a stranger, and within about fifteen seconds I will have decided whether he is trustworthy, whether she is secretly bored, and whether either of them is worth sitting next to at dinner. It is a habit I picked up years ago, and for a long time I would have defended it fiercely as a kind of instinct. Then, three years ago, a new colleague taught me otherwise.

Her name was Renata, and she joined our design team in the middle of a particularly chaotic quarter. When she walked in on her first morning, she barely made eye contact, answered my greeting with a single syllable and sat down without a word. By lunchtime I had written her off as cold, perhaps even a little arrogant. I remember telling a friend that she struck me as the sort of person who would never be a team player. Looking back, I am slightly embarrassed by how sure I was.

What I failed to notice was that she had been travelling for nearly twenty hours. She had flown in from Lisbon the night before, had been sleeping badly in a temporary flat, and was still getting used to a language she had only ever studied in books. Within a fortnight, the 'cold' colleague turned out to be quick-witted, generous with her time, and funny in a dry, understated way. She used to stay late to help the junior designers, and nobody had asked her to. By the end of the year she had become one of the people I trusted most.

Psychologists have a name for the mistake I made: the primacy effect. We give disproportionate weight to the first information we receive about someone, and we then interpret everything that follows in its light. A shy person who seems distant is read as unfriendly; a confident one who talks too much is read as big-headed. The cruel part is that the first impression is rarely a fair sample of a person. It captures how someone behaves on their worst day, in unfamiliar surroundings, under pressure, which are precisely the conditions in which most of us come across at our least impressive.

That does not mean first impressions are worthless. Research suggests that people can, in fact, pick up on a few things quickly, such as warmth and energy, though they are considerably worse at detecting honesty or reliability, which take time to reveal themselves. The practical lesson, I think, is to hold our first verdicts lightly. I now make a point of revising my opinion of anyone after a second and a third encounter, ideally in a different setting. Renata, who is now my closest friend at work, still teases me about the day I wrote her off before lunch. 'You'd made up your mind,' she says, 'before I'd even taken my coat off.' She is right, of course. She usually is. What strikes me most, in hindsight, is not that I misjudged her, but how little effort it would have taken to avoid it. A friendly question over coffee, or simply a willingness to wait a few days, would have saved us both a fortnight of needless awkwardness. These days, when someone strikes me as unfriendly or aloof, I try to ask myself a different question: what might this person be dealing with that I know nothing about?

humour that is subtle and ironic, delivered without showing emotion
restrained or modest in style, without drawing attention
much too large or too great compared with what is reasonable
to make fun of someone in a playful way
to make a deliberate effort to do something

listening.title: Small Talk: the first-impression trap
listening.intro: Listen to the podcast excerpt. You can repeat it.

lines.text: Welcome back to Small Talk, the show that picks apart the little moments that shape our lives. Today it's first impressions, and I'm joined by Priya, a recruiter, and Dan, who claims he's hopeless at them.
Hopeless is putting it mildly. I once sat through an entire interview convinced the panel hated me, simply because nobody smiled.

Oh, that happens all the time. Interviewers are often just concentrating. I'd been sitting through back-to-back interviews since eight that morning, and by the afternoon I probably looked like a statue.
So how did it go in the end, Dan?

Well, I got the job, funnily enough. It turned out the stern woman in the middle was the department head, and she used to interview people with a straight face on purpose, just to see how they'd cope.
That's a fairly common tactic. Personally, I'd never do it. It tells you more about how someone handles stress than whether they can do the job.
Priya, when a candidate walks in, what makes an impression on you straight away?
Honestly? Not the firm handshake everyone goes on about. It's whether they listen. The ones who leave a lasting impression are the ones who pick up on what I've said and build on it.
See, that's me. I tend to talk over people when I'm nervous, and I come across as a bit big-headed, even though I'm really just terrified.
And that's exactly why I always give people a second chance. Nerves can make a perfectly lovely person seem rather abrasive.
Dan, you moved to Edinburgh last year, didn't you? Have you got used to the weather yet?
Not remotely. I'm still not used to it getting dark at half past three. Back home I'd leave work in daylight all year round.
Give it time. I moved here from Mumbai ten years ago, and I'd been dreading the winters for months. Now I can't imagine living anywhere else.
On that note, let's take a short break. When we come back: how to recover from a bad first impression.

tasks.prompt: Describe a person who made a strong impression on you, first as you saw them at the beginning and then as you know them now.
questions: Who is the person and where did you meet?
What was your first impression of them?
How did that impression change over time?
What kind of person are they, in your opinion?
tasks.model: The person I have in mind is my former supervisor, Elena. When we first met, she struck me as rather cold and a touch intimidating, mainly because she hardly smiled. I had been dreading working with her for weeks. As it turned out, she was simply very focused, and underneath she was kind-hearted and remarkably level-headed. I soon warmed to her, and she's now the person I trust most at work.
checklist: Use struck me as / came across as + adjective
Include a softener (rather, a touch)
Use had been + -ing or the past perfect for what came earlier
Include two compound personality adjectives
Mark the change of opinion (as it turned out, I soon warmed to)

tasks.prompt: Tell an anecdote about an awkward or surprising first meeting.
questions: Where were you and what were you doing?
What happened out of the blue?
tasks.model: A few years ago I was queuing for a coffee when a stranger started chatting to me as if we knew each other. I was completely taken aback, but I played along. Eventually it dawned on me that he had mistaken me for his cousin. To make matters worse, I had been about to correct him just as the barista called my name, and he realised. We both burst into laughter, and, to cut a long story short, we still meet for coffee.
checklist: Past simple for the events and past continuous for the background
Past perfect for what came earlier
Two anecdote expressions (out of the blue, it dawned on me...)
Emotional reaction (taken aback, caught off guard)
Close with to cut a long story short or looking back

tasks.prompt: Discuss how reliable first impressions are, and how people adapt to a new place or job.
questions: Do you think first impressions are reliable? Why or why not?
When did you last have to get used to something new?
What helped you get used to it?
What did you use to find difficult that now feels natural?
tasks.model: In my view, first impressions are useful but far from infallible. They tell you how someone behaves under pressure, which is rarely their best. When I moved to a new city, I wasn't used to the pace of life, and it took me months to get used to commuting two hours a day. I used to find it exhausting; now I'm quite used to it, and I even use the time to read.
checklist: Be used to / get used to + -ing or noun
Used to + base for a past habit
Nuanced opinion (far from, tend to, in my view)
Clear past–present contrast

repeat: She struck me as rather reserved at first.
I had been waiting for nearly an hour.
It took me months to get used to the climate.
He's not exactly the most punctual person.
As it turned out, we had a lot in common.
Don't judge a book by its cover.
